steps.text: The last lesson was about one equation in one unknown. Now we look for the intersections of a circle with a hyperbola:
steps.explanation:
Two equations, two unknowns – but nonlinear (because of \(x^2\), \(y^2\) and \(xy\)). Gauss does not help here.

A sketch shows: there are four intersections, two in the first and two in the third quadrant. One of them is at about \((1.93,\ 0.52)\).

(This example can exceptionally be solved exactly: \(x = 2\cos 15°\), \(y = 2\sin 15°\), because then \(xy = 2 \sin 30° = 1\). We use this as a check: \(x^{*} = 1.9318516\ldots\), \(y^{*} = 0.5176381\ldots\))
steps.insight: Nonlinear systems: several equations with squares, products, sines … – no formula, no Gauss.

steps.text: As with one equation we move everything to one side. But now \(F\) is a function that maps a vector to a vector:
steps.formula: F(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} f_1(x, y) \\ f_2(x, y) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x^2 + y^2 - 4 \\ x\,y - 1 \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{!}{=} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
In general: \(F: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\), we look for \(x^{*}\) with \(F(x^{*}) = 0\) – \(n\) equations for \(n\) unknowns.

Such systems arise everywhere: force equilibria in nonlinear materials, chemical reactions, power grids, implicit methods for differential equations (lesson “Stiff ODEs & Multistep Methods”).

Our roadmap:
1. The derivative of a vector-valued function: the Jacobian matrix
2. The Newton step: one linear system per iteration
3. Convergence and the role of the starting value
4. Variants: simplified, damped and quasi-Newton
5. Gauss–Newton for nonlinear least squares problems
6. Newton for optimisation
steps.insight: We seek \(x^{*} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) with \(F(x^{*}) = 0\). Newton works here too – with matrices instead of numbers.

steps.text: As a reminder, the idea of Newton in one dimension: the function is replaced by its tangent.
steps.explanation:
In several dimensions we need:
• a replacement for the derivative \(f'\) – this will be the Jacobian matrix,
• a replacement for dividing by \(f'\) – this will be solving a linear system.

Everything else stays the same.
steps.insight: Newton = linearise and take the root of the linearisation. This works in any dimension.

steps.text: How does \(F\) change when \(x\) and \(y\) are changed a little? Each component \(f_i\) depends on both variables. The partial derivatives say how strongly:
steps.formula: DF(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y} \\[2mm] \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
This matrix is called the Jacobian matrix of \(F\).

The structure to remember:
• Row \(i\) belongs to the function \(f_i\) (to equation \(i\)).
• Column \(j\) belongs to the variable we differentiate with respect to.

You can find more about partial derivatives in the lesson “Multidimensional Calculus”.
steps.insight: Jacobian matrix: row = function, column = variable. Entry \((i, j)\) is \(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\).

steps.text: For our example:
steps.formula: F = \begin{pmatrix} x^2 + y^2 - 4 \\ x\,y - 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad DF = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 2y \\ y & x \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
Entry by entry:
• \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2 + y^2 - 4) = 2x\) (\(y\) is treated as a constant)
• \(\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2 + y^2 - 4) = 2y\)
• \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xy - 1) = y\)
• \(\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy - 1) = x\)

At the point \((2,\ 0.5)\): \(DF = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0.5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\).
steps.insight: Setting up the Jacobian: differentiate each equation partially with respect to each variable.

steps.text: The Jacobian matrix provides the linearisation – the multidimensional tangent:
steps.explanation:
Check with the example: at \(x = (2,\ 0.5)\), \(F = (0.25,\ 0)\). We move a little in the \(x\) direction: \(\Delta = (0.1,\ 0)\).

• Linearisation: \((0.25, 0) + \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0.5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0.1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = (0.25 + 0.4,\ 0 + 0.05) = (0.65,\ 0.05)\)
• Exact: \(F(2.1,\ 0.5) = (4.41 + 0.25 - 4,\ 1.05 - 1) = (0.66,\ 0.05)\)

Very close! The small difference (\(0.01\)) is the quadratic part \(0.1^2\) that the linearisation leaves out.
steps.insight: \(F(x + \Delta) \approx F(x) + DF(x)\Delta\) – the more accurate, the smaller \(\Delta\).

steps.text: Quick check: determine the Jacobian matrix of
steps.formula: F(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} x^2 - y \\ \sin x + y^3 \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
• Row 1: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2 - y) = 2x\), \(\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2 - y) = -1\)
• Row 2: \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sin x + y^3) = \cos x\), \(\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sin x + y^3) = 3y^2\)

\(DF = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & -1 \\ \cos x & 3y^2 \end{pmatrix}\)

Typical mistake: swapping rows and columns, i.e. writing down the transpose.
steps.insight: Check question: does row 1 really contain only derivatives of the first equation?

steps.text: With three unknowns it works the same way. Example:
steps.formula: F(x, y, z) = \begin{pmatrix} x + y + z - 3 \\ x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 5 \\ x\,y\,z - 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad DF = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2x & 2y & 2z \\ yz & xz & xy \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
Each row is the gradient of one equation:
• Row 1: all three variables appear with factor \(1\).
• Row 2: the derivative of \(x^2\) with respect to \(x\) is \(2x\), and so on.
• Row 3: differentiating \(xyz\) with respect to \(x\) leaves \(y\) and \(z\): \(yz\).

At the point \((1, 1, 1)\): \(DF = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) – singular (all rows are multiples of each other). So this point would be a bad starting value.
steps.insight: Row \(i\) of the Jacobian matrix is the gradient of the \(i\)-th equation.

steps.text: Now the Newton step: we require the linearisation to vanish.
steps.explanation:
Instead of dividing by \(f'\) one solves a linear system with the Jacobian matrix. Formally \(\Delta = -DF(x_k)^{-1} F(x_k)\) – but the inverse is never computed explicitly (see “Gaussian Elimination & LU Decomposition”).

The method per step:
1. Evaluate \(F(x_k)\).
2. Set up \(DF(x_k)\).
3. Solve the linear system \(DF(x_k)\,\Delta = -F(x_k)\) (Gauss with pivoting).
4. \(x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta\).
5. Check whether \(\|\Delta\|\) or \(\|F(x_{k+1})\|\) is small enough.
steps.insight: Newton for systems: solve \(DF(x_k)\Delta = -F(x_k)\), then \(x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta\).

steps.text: The first step for our example with starting value \(x_0 = (2,\ 0.5)\):
steps.explanation:
Solve the \(2 \times 2\) system (e.g. with Cramer's rule, perfectly fine for \(2 \times 2\) by hand):
• \(\det = 4 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 0.5 = 7.5\)
• \(\Delta_1 = \frac{(-0.25) \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 0}{7.5} = -\frac{0.5}{7.5} \approx -0.0667\)
• \(\Delta_2 = \frac{4 \cdot 0 - 0.5 \cdot (-0.25)}{7.5} = \frac{0.125}{7.5} \approx 0.0167\)

New point: \(x_1 = (2 - 0.0667,\ 0.5 + 0.0167) = (1.9333,\ 0.5167)\).

Comparison with the solution \((1.93185,\ 0.51764)\): the error has dropped from \(0.068\) to \(0.0015\).
steps.insight: A Newton step by hand: evaluate \(F\) and \(DF\), solve a \(2 \times 2\) system, add.

steps.text: The second step, starting from \(x_1 = (1.93333,\ 0.51667)\):
steps.insight: After just two steps, 6 digits are correct.

steps.text: Geometrically, Newton replaces both curves by their tangents at the current point and jumps to their intersection:
steps.explanation:
The animation deliberately starts further away, at \(x_0 = (3,\ 0.2)\), so the steps are easy to see:
• The tangent to the circle and the tangent to the hyperbola at \(x_0\) are two lines.
• Their intersection is \(x_1 = (2.147,\ 0.390)\) – exactly the solution of the linear system \(DF\,\Delta = -F\).
• After that it goes fast: \(x_2 = (1.949,\ 0.502)\), \(x_3 = (1.9320,\ 0.5174)\), \(x_4 = (1.93185,\ 0.51764)\).

Just as in one dimension the tangent crosses the \(x\)-axis, here the “tangents” of the two equations intersect.
steps.insight: Newton in 2D: linearise both equations (tangents) and take their intersection.

steps.text: What does one Newton step cost with \(n\) unknowns?
steps.explanation:
• Evaluate \(F(x_k)\): \(n\) functions.
• Set up \(DF(x_k)\): \(n^2\) partial derivatives. Often the most expensive part – especially if they have to be approximated numerically by difference quotients.
• Solve the linear system: about \(\frac{2}{3}n^3\) operations with Gauss (much fewer for sparse Jacobians, or iteratively).

For \(n = 2\) all this is trivial. For \(n = 10\,000\) every Newton step is a serious computation. That is why there are variants that save work (Chapter 5).
steps.insight: One Newton step costs: function + Jacobian + one linear system.

steps.text: Quick check: perform one Newton step with starting value \((0, 0)\) for the following (linear!) system. What do you notice?
steps.formula: F(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} x + y - 3 \\ x - y - 1 \end{pmatrix}
steps.explanation:
\(F(0, 0) = (-3, -1)\), \(DF = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) (constant).

\(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\Delta = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\): adding the rows gives \(2\Delta_1 = 4\), so \(\Delta_1 = 2\), \(\Delta_2 = 1\).

\(x_1 = (2, 1)\). Check: \(2 + 1 - 3 = 0\) ✓, \(2 - 1 - 1 = 0\) ✓

For a linear system Newton is exact after one step – because the linearisation is then the system itself.
steps.insight: If \(F\) is linear, Newton finds the solution in a single step.

steps.text: The errors of our example with start \((2,\ 0.5)\):
steps.explanation:
As in one dimension: the exponent of the error roughly doubles – quadratic convergence.

The theorem: if \(F\) is twice continuously differentiable and the Jacobian is invertible at the solution (\(\det DF(x^{*}) \neq 0\)), then Newton converges quadratically for starting values close enough to \(x^{*}\).

In our example: \(\det DF(x^{*}) = 2x^2 - 2y^2 \approx 2 \cdot 3.732 - 2 \cdot 0.268 \approx 6.93 \neq 0\) ✓
steps.insight: Newton for systems converges locally quadratically if \(DF(x^{*})\) is invertible.

steps.text: Which of the four intersections Newton finds depends on the starting value. Let's start at \((1,\ 1.5)\):
steps.explanation:
This time Newton lands at the intersection \((0.5176,\ 1.9319)\) – the mirror image in the diagonal.

The first step jumps far (to \(x = 0.10\)) because the tangents fit poorly at the start. After that it is quadratic.

In general the space of starting values splits into basins of attraction: from each basin Newton runs to one particular solution. The boundaries between these basins can be very complicated (fractal). If you want a particular solution, you need a good starting value – for example from a sketch or an approximation.
steps.insight: The starting value determines which solution Newton finds – or whether it finds one at all.

steps.text: What happens if \(DF\) is singular? Let's try the starting value \((1,\ 1)\):
steps.explanation:
The linear system \(DF\,\Delta = -F\) then has no unique solution; Newton breaks down.

Geometrically: at the point \((1, 1)\) the tangents to the circle and hyperbola are parallel – they have no intersection.

An almost singular Jacobian is dangerous too: then the Newton step is huge (like the horizontal tangent in one dimension) and lands anywhere. This is the same problem as with ill-conditioned linear systems.
steps.insight: Singular or almost singular Jacobian ⇒ Newton step undefined or huge.

steps.text: Quick check: for which points \((x, y)\) is the Jacobian of our example singular?
steps.explanation:
\(\det DF = \det \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 2y \\ y & x \end{pmatrix} = 2x^2 - 2y^2 = 2(x - y)(x + y)\)

So \(DF\) is singular when \(y = x\) or \(y = -x\) – on the two diagonals.

That fits: these lines contain the points where the circle and hyperbola tangents are parallel. Starting values near these lines are bad, because the first step jumps very far.
steps.insight: \(\det DF = 0\) describes the “dangerous” starting values.

steps.text: When do you stop? As in one dimension, just with norms:
steps.explanation:
• The length of the Newton step \(\|\Delta_k\|\) is a good estimate of the current error: thanks to quadratic convergence the next error is much smaller. In the example: \(\|\Delta_2\|_\infty \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the error of \(x_2\) is also about \(1.1 \cdot 10^{-6}\).
• The residual \(\|F\|\) shows how well the equations are satisfied.
• Always also a maximum number of steps – in case Newton does not converge.

Tip: if the equations are scaled very differently (one in metres, one in millimetres), bring them to a similar magnitude first, otherwise one equation dominates the norm.
steps.insight: Stop: small Newton step, small residual, or maximum number of steps reached.

steps.text: Setting up and factorising the Jacobian in every step is expensive. The simplified Newton method always uses the Jacobian at the starting value:
steps.explanation:
Advantage: \(DF(x_0)\) is factorised with LU only once. Each further step costs only forward and back substitution, i.e. \(O(n^2)\) instead of \(O(n^3)\).

Disadvantage: convergence is only linear. For our example with start \((2,\ 0.5)\):
errors \(1.5 \cdot 10^{-3},\ 7.4 \cdot 10^{-5},\ 4.1 \cdot 10^{-6},\ 2.3 \cdot 10^{-7},\ 1.3 \cdot 10^{-8}\)

Each step reduces the error by about a factor of \(0.05\). That is slower than Newton (which was at \(10^{-12}\) after 3 steps), but each step is much cheaper. For large systems this often pays off.
steps.insight: Simplified Newton: freeze the Jacobian. Cheaper steps, but only linear convergence.

steps.text: Against bad starting values the damped Newton method helps. You take only part of the Newton step:
steps.explanation:
How do you choose \(\lambda_k\)? A simple strategy (step halving):
1. Try \(\lambda = 1\) (full Newton step).
2. If \(\|F(x_k + \lambda\Delta_k)\| < \|F(x_k)\|\), accept.
3. Otherwise halve \(\lambda\) and try again.

The idea: the Newton direction always points “downhill” for \(\|F\|^2\). A small step in this direction therefore surely improves things. Only the full step can be too far.

Close to the solution \(\lambda = 1\) is accepted automatically, and quadratic convergence returns.
steps.insight: Damped Newton: halve the step until \(\|F\|\) decreases. Makes Newton much more robust.

steps.text: And if the partial derivatives are not known at all? Two ways out:
steps.explanation:
• Difference quotients: column \(j\) of the Jacobian is approximated by
\(\frac{F(x + h\,e_j) - F(x)}{h}\)
This costs \(n\) additional evaluations of \(F\) per step. Choosing \(h\) is a trade-off (see “Conditioning & Stability”, \(h \approx \sqrt{u}\)).

• Quasi-Newton methods (e.g. Broyden): start with an approximation of the Jacobian and update it in every step by a simple correction (of rank 1), so that the approximation correctly reproduces the most recently observed change \(F(x_{k+1}) - F(x_k)\). This is the multidimensional version of the secant method. Convergence is superlinear.
steps.insight: Without derivatives: approximate the Jacobian by difference quotients or use quasi-Newton (Broyden).

steps.text: In the lesson “Least Squares & QR Decomposition” we made the model \(y = a\,e^{bt}\) linear by taking logarithms. But that minimises the errors of \(\ln y\), not of \(y\). Now we solve the actual problem:
steps.explanation:
The residuals \(r_i(a, b) = a\,e^{bt_i} - y_i\) depend nonlinearly on \(b\). This is a nonlinear least squares problem: more equations (data points) than unknowns (parameters), and nonlinear.

Data as before: \((0;\ 2.0)\), \((1;\ 5.5)\), \((2;\ 14.7)\).
steps.insight: Nonlinear least squares problem: \(\min \|r(p)\|_2^2\), where the residuals depend nonlinearly on the parameters \(p\).

steps.text: The idea of the Gauss–Newton method: linearise the residuals (as in Newton) and then solve a linear least squares problem (as in least squares fitting).
steps.explanation:
Here \(J\) is the Jacobian of the residuals: row \(i\) belongs to data point \(i\), column \(j\) to parameter \(j\). For \(r_i = a\,e^{bt_i} - y_i\):
• \(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial a} = e^{bt_i}\)
• \(\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial b} = a\,t_i\,e^{bt_i}\)

So each Gauss–Newton step is a linear least squares problem – solvable with the normal equations or (more stably) with QR.
steps.insight: Gauss–Newton: linearise the residuals, solve a linear least squares problem for the step, repeat.

steps.text: What does a Gauss–Newton step look like concretely? At the starting value \(a_0 = 2.0095\), \(b_0 = 0.99735\) we compute residuals and Jacobian:
steps.explanation:
Columns 4 and 5 form the \(3 \times 2\) matrix \(J\), column 3 is the residual vector \(r\).

Then one solves the linear least squares problem \(\min \|J\Delta + r\|_2\), for example via the normal equations \(J^{T}J\,\Delta = -J^{T}r\) – exactly as in the lesson “Least Squares & QR Decomposition”, just with \(J\) instead of \(A\) and \(-r\) instead of \(b\).

The result is the correction \(\Delta \approx (0.0272,\ -0.0090)\) for \((a, b)\).
steps.insight: One Gauss–Newton step = a table of residuals and derivatives + one linear least squares problem.

steps.text: We start with the values from the logarithmic approach: \(a_0 = 2.0095\), \(b_0 = 0.99735\).
steps.explanation:
After just one step the sum of squares has dropped to almost a quarter; after that hardly anything changes.

Result: \(y \approx 2.037\,e^{0.988\,t}\) instead of \(y \approx 2.010\,e^{0.997\,t}\) from the logarithmic approach.

The difference is small, but the new model is the “right” one in the least squares sense for \(y\). Typical procedure: get a starting value from a linearisation of the model, then refine with Gauss–Newton.
steps.insight: Good starting values for Gauss–Newton often come from a linearisation of the model (e.g. taking logarithms).

steps.text: How does Gauss–Newton compare with Newton?
steps.explanation:
• Gauss–Newton needs only first derivatives (the matrix \(J\)). Newton for the minimum of \(S\) would need second derivatives.
• If the model fits the data well (small residuals), Gauss–Newton converges almost quadratically – as in our example.
• With large residuals or bad starting values it can become slow or diverge.

The robust variant is the Levenberg–Marquardt method: it solves \((J^{T}J + \mu I)\Delta = -J^{T}r\). A large \(\mu\) makes small, cautious steps (almost like gradient descent), a small \(\mu\) makes Gauss–Newton steps. \(\mu\) is adapted automatically. Almost every curve-fitting software uses this method.
steps.insight: Levenberg–Marquardt = Gauss–Newton with built-in damping. The standard for nonlinear curve fitting.

steps.text: Newton has one more important application: minimising functions of several variables. At a minimum the gradient is zero:
steps.explanation:
That is a nonlinear system \(F(x) = \nabla f(x) = 0\)! Applying Newton to it, the Jacobian of \(\nabla f\) is the matrix of second derivatives, the Hessian matrix \(H_f\).

So the Newton step for optimisation reads:
\(H_f(x_k)\,\Delta = -\nabla f(x_k)\), \(x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta\)

Intuitively: approximate \(f\) by a quadratic function (Taylor to second order) and jump to its minimum.
steps.insight: Newton for optimisation: \(H_f\,\Delta = -\nabla f\). The Hessian takes the role of the Jacobian.

steps.text: An example: minimise \(f(x, y) = x^4 + y^2 - 2x\).
steps.explanation:
Start \((1, 1)\):
• \(\nabla f = (2,\ 2)\), \(H_f = \begin{pmatrix} 12 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\)
• \(\Delta = \left(-\frac{2}{12},\ -\frac{2}{2}\right) = (-0.1667,\ -1)\)
• \(x_1 = (0.8333,\ 0)\)

In \(y\) you are done at once (there \(f\) is exactly quadratic). In \(x\): \(0.8333 \to 0.79556 \to 0.793705 \to 0.7937005\). The minimum is at \(x = \sqrt[3]{0.5} \approx 0.7937005\) ✓

A note: Newton finds points with \(\nabla f = 0\) – these can also be maxima or saddle points. That is why one checks whether the Hessian is positive definite (here yes: \(12x^2 > 0\) and \(2 > 0\)).
steps.insight: Newton optimisation converges quadratically to critical points. The Hessian shows whether it is a minimum.

steps.text: Quick check: apply one Newton step to \(f(x, y) = x^2 + xy + y^2 - 3x\), start \((0, 0)\). How many steps does Newton need to reach the minimum?
steps.explanation:
\(\nabla f = (2x + y - 3,\ x + 2y)\), \(H_f = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) (constant).

At the start: \(\nabla f(0, 0) = (-3, 0)\). Solve \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\Delta = (3, 0)\): \(\det = 3\), \(\Delta_1 = \frac{6}{3} = 2\), \(\Delta_2 = \frac{-3}{3} = -1\).

\(x_1 = (2, -1)\). Check: \(\nabla f(2, -1) = (4 - 1 - 3,\ 2 - 2) = (0, 0)\) ✓

A single step! For quadratic functions the second-order Taylor approximation is exact, so Newton jumps straight to the minimum. This is the counterpart of “linear system in one step” from Chapter 3.
steps.insight: For quadratic functions Newton finds the minimum in one step.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Set up nonlinear systems \(F(x) = 0\) with \(F: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\).

2. Jacobian matrix \(DF\): entry \((i, j)\) is \(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\). Linearisation \(F(x + \Delta) \approx F(x) + DF(x)\Delta\).

3. Newton step: solve \(DF(x_k)\Delta = -F(x_k)\), \(x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta\). Locally quadratic if \(DF(x^{*})\) is invertible.

4. The starting value decides which solution is found. Singular Jacobian ⇒ breakdown.

5. Variants: simplified Newton (freeze the Jacobian, linear), damped Newton (halve the step), quasi-Newton (Broyden, superlinear).

6. Gauss–Newton for \(\min \|r(p)\|_2\): \(J^{T}J\Delta = -J^{T}r\). Robust: Levenberg–Marquardt.

7. Newton for optimisation: \(H_f\Delta = -\nabla f\).
steps.insight: Key message: Newton in \(n\) dimensions = linearise with the Jacobian + one linear system per step.

steps.text: What comes next? This lesson ends the block on equations. Next we turn to functions themselves: how do you find a function that passes through given data points?
steps.explanation:
In the lesson “Polynomial Interpolation” you will learn how to put exactly one polynomial of degree \(n\) through \(n + 1\) points – with the Lagrange and Newton forms – and why high polynomial degrees can be dangerous (Runge's phenomenon).

Newton's method and linearisation will meet you again later: in implicit methods for differential equations, where a nonlinear system has to be solved in every time step.
steps.insight: Next block: approximating functions – interpolation, splines, quadrature.
